This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New research demonstrates that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.
  • The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.
  • Both measures were linked to mortality risk and highlighted similar ability to predict it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New research demonstrates that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and highlighted similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

It has been revealed that for free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

According to recent reports, from this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:.

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own revealed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Recent findings suggest that overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, remarked that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”.

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

According to recent reports, “It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” mentioned Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she noted.

In a recent development, theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he stated.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

According to recent reports, “Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he mentioned. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have complications with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

According to recent reports, “I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being vital,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

Tech Report: Endangered, colorful garter snakes released into the wild for the first time

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most people have never seen a San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia).
  • Sources indicate that however, conservationists recently scored a major win for the snakes.
  • “Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work,” Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen) biologist Karine Tokatlian noted in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most people have never seen a San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia). Native only to California’s San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties, the brilliantly colored reptile was one of the initial entries in the United States Fish and Wildlife Service’s first endangered species list in 1967. After nearly 60 more years of droughts, invasive species, disease, low genetic diversity, and poaching, researchers estimate only a few thousand San Francisco garter snakes still exist in the wild.

Sources indicate that however, conservationists recently scored a major win for the snakes. For the first time, 62 of young serpents born at the San Francisco Zoo were released at specific sites across San Mateo County earlier this fall. The successful rewilding of dozens of the endangered snakes marks a huge moment for population rehabilitation efforts, and hopefully clears the way for similar releases in the future.

“Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work,” Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen) biologist Karine Tokatlian noted in a statement. “This first release is an vital step toward building healthy, resilient populations that can sustain themselves over the long term.”.

Recent findings suggest that although slender, the brightly colored San Francisco garter snake can grow anywhere from 18 to 55 inches long. Its eyes are larger than most of its fellow garter snakes, allowing it to keep active during daylight hours. With no fangs and only mildly toxic saliva, the snake is essentially harmless to humans, although its bites are fatal for prey like smaller reptiles and rodents.

According to recent reports, the process of releasing young animals like these snakes that were reared in captivity is known as head-starting. It is an effective way to protect creatures during the most vulnerable stage of their lives. Head-starting the first batch of San Francisco garter snakes began in 2025, when conservationists collected multiple pregnant females from a healthy preserve in California’s Midpeninsula. Researchers later released the adult snakes back into their habitats after they gave birth, but kept the infants at the San Francisco Zoo. While there, zoologists conducted genetic testing on each snake to select the best possible locations for their eventual release. Conservationists deposited about one-third of them in the same area as their mothers, then placed the other two-thirds at locations particularly in need of greater genetic diversity pools for breeding.

As biologists continue to monitor the first generation of head-started snakes, another generation is already waiting for its time to shine. More than 130 garter snakes have been born at the San Francisco Zoo this year alone, with an eye to release them sometime in 2027.

“This species is special in many ways, but unfortunately its critical status is not unique,” added Midpen wildlife ecologist Ariel Starr. “The success of this project and the associated research will not only benefit the San Francisco garter snake but will also hopefully inform the recovery of many imperiled reptile species.”.

High altitude, bitter cold, zero drivers: autonomous trucks take on Tibetan mine

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.
  • Chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

Chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

“High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”.

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the manufacturer won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the substantial bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

“Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”.

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is at the moment operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

Industry observers note that while specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the company has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The massive trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

Mercedes’s Latest Tesla-Style Point-to-Point Drive Pilot System Is Useful But Not Quite Convincing

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sitting in the leftmost of two left-turn lanes in a newly introduced Mercedes-Benz GLC EV, I notice something strange.
  • Thankfully, the visible indecision turns into the right choice.
  • According to recent reports, after the drive, a Mercedes engineer told Road & Track that this could have been a result of disagreement between the priorities of two different systems that go into the MB.Drive-branded point-to-point navigation system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sitting in the leftmost of two left-turn lanes in a newly introduced Mercedes-Benz GLC EV, I notice something strange. I can see my right turn signal on in the reflection of the car in front of me. Then I see my left signal, then my right again. This is less than a mile into an hour testing a new “Level 2++” ADAS system set to be rolled out by Mercedes, and I have ceded control to what seems to be a hesitant computer that seems to be second-guessing itself.

Thankfully, the visible indecision turns into the right choice. The system turns left from the lane, continues on its planned route, and eventually takes a right a quarter-mile later as it had originally intended.

According to recent reports, after the drive, a Mercedes engineer told Road & Track that this could have been a result of disagreement between the priorities of two different systems that go into the MB.Drive-branded point-to-point navigation system. Since the Mercedes ADAS suite uses both the Alpamayo AI model built by Mercedes autonomy partner Nvidia and a “classical stack” of more hard-coded priorities, the engineer inferred that the signal interaction could have been a result of a disagreement between the systems.

It has been revealed that the engineer reckoned that the system was trying to think ahead, with the best way to plan for a future right turn being to be in the rightmost of the two left turn lanes. Hence the sudden desire to go one over—a point of conflict. Sometimes, he said, the classical path and the end-to-end model end up in conflict. A more cynical take? That our new robot overlords are already fighting each other.

The interaction was a particularly odd experience in San Francisco. I work in the city and encounter more advanced self-driving pilot programs from companies like Zoox and Waymo every day. Seeing a Waymo Ojai van in traffic at the same stoplight, I thought about how the “Level 2++” Mercedes system seems to be far off the cutting edge being explored at the global hub of automated taxi development.

Fortunately, that turn-signal confusion never came up again. For the most part, the GLC navigated the busy and often unpredictable streets of San Francisco just before evening rush hour without any need for intervention. I actually deactivated the system just once, to take control the first time I came across a widely parked car in a corner. I otherwise trusted it to figure out everything from jaywalkers to chicanes made of two separate double-parked cars a hundred or so feet apart on opposite sides of a tight road. If I had come across the same parking matter later in the drive, I would have trusted the system without taking over.

Recent findings suggest that other than the confusion at that first intersection, most of my frustrations with the system came from its combination of cautiousness and aggression. Overly-patient ADAS programming is certainly not a bad thing, but I was regularly met with confusion by motorists at stop signs who wondered why the car took so long to get going after coming to a complete stop.

It has been revealed that the system’s decision-making with pedestrians would usually be similarly cautious, as it was when the car slowed for someone waiting for a light to cross well within the bounds of a sidewalk. That person was kicking in the air, something that I inferred the car would pick up as a sign that they might start walking soon, so I let the system make its incorrect guess and slowed from around 35 mph to about 10 mph.

Sources indicate that calculations about pedestrians were not always cautious, though. A few miles later, the system opted to enter an intersection while a slower pedestrian crossed after the light turned green. It came surprisingly close to the pedestrian, still well within a safe distance but nearer than I would have driven personally. This felt a bit unnerving with the car’s high beltline and relatively low visibility over the front fenders, but I never came close enough to have to slam on the brakes and take complete control back.

Industry observers note that this is a hands-on system that Mercedes still describes as Level 2 autonomy, even if their 2++ designation obfuscates that fact. It is not true autonomous driving, so I followed the guidelines and kept my hands on the wheel and eyes on the road. The closest comparison is Tesla’s absurdly named Full Self-Driving. When this releases, Mercedes hopes to be among the first legacy automakers to directly rival the younger EV brands in this space.

In addition to the headlining point-to-point navigation system, Mercedes allowed us to test a forthcoming hands-free ADAS system available for on-highway use in an S-class and again in a GLE crossover. Unlike the city-driving component, this system allows drivers to completely disengage their hands and feet. It still requires eyes on the road and will aggressively chirp at you to get your hands back on the wheel if you spend too long adjusting a passenger-side mirror. I learned that lesson firsthand, the only time the system forced me to get my eyes back on the road in about 30 miles of highway testing over the two different cars.

According to recent reports, this system felt little different from the usual MB.Drive-branded adaptive cruise control. I took control once on this stretch, when the GLE test car signaled to enter a middle lane that a Ram 2500 with a massive trailer was already signaling to enter from the other lane. The system would probably have figured out its own mistake before this became a problem, but I disengaged it entirely and overrode the lane change before I found out how long that would take.

Recent findings suggest that while both systems are temporarily coming for free to select Mercedes models in California as part of an early-access program in December, final pricing and a nationwide rollout for either system remain to be determined. Hands-free highway assist is planned to reach consumers in spring of next year, available to cars on the MB.OS platform with the existing MB.Drive Assist option package.

Point-to-point navigation, the Tesla-style system for in-city driving, will be available as a subscription model. Mercedes says it is coming to cars operating on the brand’s most modern MB.OS-branded architecture starting at some point in 2027. We know that it will be available as a three-year subscription from the factory and in one-year or one-month increments from the car’s digital storefront. Pricing has not been finalized, but a representative from the firm claims that it will be “competitive” with comparable offerings from brands like Tesla.

In a recent development, for buyers who prioritize tech that are already looking at one of the products that will be getting the new ADAS suite, the Mercedes system should be worth the eventual subscription price. Given the subscription-only offering and cautious nature of the point-to-point offering, buyers content to drive themselves around a city for a few more years will not be missing out if they opt to forego the new service.

Battlefield 6 streamlines some of the most annoying Challenges yet again, takes out a few of them entirely

📅 20 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 2 min read (374 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Vg247

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done.
  • This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.
  • The updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done. Having just released a latest patch - which already included several updates to Challenges and Assignments - Battlefield Studios has gone in and made even more changes.

This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.

The updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge. Now, any headshot beyond 75m will count. Recon Expert 3 is another headshot-themed one that’s been updated, and now requires getting headshot kills beyond 125m, rather than the practically impossible beyond 200m that it required previously.

Sources indicate that the Rapid Fire 2 Challenge, which required getting kills beyond 50m with Assault Rifles, has been changed so it now tracks anything beyond 40m. The painful ‘Inflict damage under 15m while hip-firing with Assault Rifles’ has been entirely replaced with one that requires - the far more sensible - inflicting damage while in ADS with Assault Rifles.

A couple of Challenges, such as the one that required suppressing enemies with LMGs, and another that wanted you to deal damage to laser-designated vehicles using lock-on weapons, have both been removed.

The journey to make Challenges and Assignments easier to complete has been a long one. Progression has been one of the key areas of criticism Battlefield 6 received at launch. The matter encompassed more than just slow player and weapon XP earn rates, it also prevented players from accessing new Training Paths for the various classes, and several of the game's weapons.

Battlefield Studios attacked the problem from multiple angles, initially boosting the XP players and their weapons would earn, before later reducing the requirements of the Challenges themselves. The developer continued to streamline those requirements over multiple patches, including majorly overhauling the system earlier this month.

It seems the studio is more confident than ever in the game, as it recently revealed that Battlefield 6 will be getting its first free trial next week, offering players who do not own the full game access to iconic modes like Conquest, and Breakthrough - though on an unusual selection of maps.

#5437. How I Had to Learn to Stop Saying “Yes” When I Meant “No”

How I Had to Learn to Stop Saying “Yes” When I Meant “No”

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • For years, I was a girl who would say “yes” when I meant “no.” It was only after I decided to stop drinking that I realized how much my “yes-girl” tendency had fueled my drinking cycle over the years.
  • Over the years, both through my own recovery and my work in helping others break their drinking patterns, I have come to see that most people who eventually come to question their relationship with alcohol don’t have a “drinking problem;” instead, they have a “drinking solution.” In my case, my inability and unwillingness to say “no” had created a lot of problems that I ended up turning to alcohol to solve.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

For years, I was a girl who would say “yes” when I meant “no.” It was only after I decided to stop drinking that I realized how much my “yes-girl” tendency had fueled my drinking cycle over the years.

Over the years, both through my own recovery and my work in helping others break their drinking patterns, I have come to see that most people who eventually come to question their relationship with alcohol don’t have a “drinking problem;” instead, they have a “drinking solution.” In my case, my inability and unwillingness to say “no” had created a lot of problems that I ended up turning to alcohol to solve.

Recent findings suggest that I would say yes to a football weekend marathon when I didn’t even know what a quarterback was, and then turn to a 6-pack to make time pass faster. I would say “yes” to hosting the relative whom I couldn't stand, then try to push away my resentment with a bottle of wine. I would say “yes” to helping out at a neighbor’s garage sale after a long week and end up trying to recover from exhaustion with a few cocktails.

As I started to help others break their old drinking patterns, I realized I was far from the only person who got caught in this pattern. In fact, I came to nickname this particular drinking pattern “the Yes-Effect Drinking Loop.” It’s one of the 10 most common invisible drinking loops that keep an unwanted drinking pattern alive.

Industry observers note that in most unhealthy drinking patterns, drinking is only what we see on the surface. The Invisible Drinking Loop is a term I created to help people understand the hidden forces that keep their drinking patterns alive. An invisible drinking loop is often driven by the need to solve a problem, fueled by the belief that alcohol can help, and maintained by the habit loop in which drinking has become the default routine to cope with or deal with certain situations or emotions.

In the “Yes-Effect Drinking Loop,” drinking has become the solution to deal with the side effects that arise when a person struggles to say no.

As is true with most drinking loops, simply stopping drinking doesn’t break the loop.

With alcohol out of my life, I found myself sitting through events that I had no interest in, battling the desire to reach for a drink to make time pass faster, hanging out with people whose firm I didn’t enjoy, missing the quick mental escape alcohol could offer, and dealing with overwhelming cravings by the end of the day after I once again stretched myself too thin in the effort to please others instead of honoring my own limitations.

Recent findings suggest that it took me a long time to realize that simply stopping drinking doesn’t solve the problems; instead, it exposes them. I needed to learn to find another way to address the problem that I once attempted to solve through drinking, and that meant learning how to say no.

In a recent development, learning to say no after years of saying yes is not easy. When faced with a choice between disappointing others and disappointing myself, my default response was to choose the latter. Somewhere along the line, I had been conditioned to believe that fulfilling others’ expectations, even those of people whom I wasn't even that close to, was a way to keep myself safe, liked, and in good standing.

Yet, I failed to see the hidden cost of all the efforts to keep others happy; I kept myself unhappy. So much so that alcohol became the only way I knew how to push down my disappointment, exhaustion, and resentment.

Learning to say “no” started with a radical decision to honor my own preferences rather than automatically prioritize others’ expectations. Don’t get me wrong, it doesn’t mean becoming self-centered or never making compromises in life. But it does mean taking an intentional pause before giving in to my compulsive need to keep others happy. And when faced with the choice between disappointing others and disappointing myself, I wanted to make that choice consciously, rather than by default.

Of course, giving myself permission to say no was one thing. Actually knowing how to say it was another. After years of automatically saying yes, saying no felt like a skill I had not yet learned.

That's why Skill Expansion is one of the core pillars of my approach to breaking an old drinking pattern. Truly growing beyond alcohol often requires us to develop new skills and tools to navigate the challenges we once relied on alcohol to handle. For the Yes-Effect Drinking Loop, learning to say no is one of those skills.

Fortunately, like most skills, saying no is something we can learn through practice. Personally, I've found that having a few ready-to-use ways to say no makes a world of difference. That's why I've put together 7 of my favorite scripts for saying no with grace.

Latest Update: Apple HomeView smart home hub review: Siri gets a swanky new house

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • In a recent development, apple’s $299 smart display has been sitting on my kitchen counter for about a week.
  • Sources indicate that the HomeView comes in two versions, and both cost $299 in the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

In a recent development, apple’s $299 smart display has been sitting on my kitchen counter for about a week. It looks like a hybrid between an old-school iMac and a giant Apple Watch, but it’s a dedicated home for the recently revamped Siri. It’s an easy addition for anyone already committed to Apple gear. If your smart home runs on cameras, locks, or sensors that don’t work with Apple Home, though, you’ll want an upgrade strategy before you buy one.

Sources indicate that the HomeView comes in two versions, and both cost $299 in the US. I tested the tabletop model, which mounts a 7-inch square touchscreen on a domed aluminum speaker base and includes a 30W power adapter and USB-C cable in the box. You can have it in any color you want, as long as it’s silver, starlight, rose pink, or space gray. The Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) drops the base and its extra speaker hardware, as well as the starlight/rose pink color options, and the panel costs more to put on a wall than its sticker price suggests. It requires a Schneider Home mount sold separately, and those start at $59.95. The cheapest USB-C mount also needs a power adapter of at least 20W, which you’ll have to supply yourself.

The HomeView looks the way you’d expect an Apple product to look. Once you take off the protective coverings, the 2.1-pound, 6.82-inch tall device is pretty right out of the box. And it looks great between a breadbox and a butcher’s block, especially compared to an older smart screen that I’ve had there for years, which looks ancient next to it. A stainless steel hinge connects the screen to the base, so you can tilt the display toward wherever you’re standing. The screen stays firmly in place after you position it, even if you tap aggressively like I tend to. It doesn’t wobble or shake as you navigate on-screen menus.

It has been revealed that setting up the HomeView feels like setting up an iPhone or any other recent Apple device. It requires an iPhone running iOS 27.2 or later (or an iPad on iPadOS 27.2), so if your phone isn’t there yet, like mine wasn’t, you’ve got to stop and run the update first. The HomeView played a soft, heavenly drone the whole time it waited, which is a much nicer way to sit through a software update than staring at a progress bar. Also, when you first boot things up, you might think you can immediately start asking for the kind of stuff you ask Siri on your iPhone, but you may have to go through a round or two of launching apps on the HomeView to give them permission to access your account even if your iPhone is with you.

The HomeView’s Liquid Retina LED backlit screen has looked great in every lighting condition I’ve put it in. Apple rates the 1088-by-1088-pixel (220 ppi) display’s brightness between 0.3 and 500 nits, and that bottom end is what makes it work on a nightstand. In a dark kitchen, it reads as a soft glow instead of a floodlight.

Recent findings suggest that the multitouch True Tone touchscreen responds promptly, and it kept registering taps even when my fingers were slightly wet (even though the device doesn’t have a specific water-resistance rating). That’s a real advantage for a screen that spends its life in a kitchen.

The new, more conversational Siri AI on the HomeView is a massive jump from the old Siri. The HomeView’s four-mic design ensures Siri can hear you from throughout the room and, when a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone is nearby, it can pull from personal data. If you ask about an upcoming concert, it can also check the calendar on your Apple account and tell whether you’re actually free to go.

In a recent development, that personal access runs through the HomeView’s 12MP Center Stage camera. It can recognize up to six Home app-registered household members by face, and it only highlights someone’s personal information when it recognizes that person and their paired iPhone or iPad is on the same Wi-Fi network—with support for Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) with MIMO—and was recently unlocked. The HomeView’s A18 chip uses what Apple calls Secure Exclaves to process the camera and microphone feeds in a separate compartment, and Apple states neither the operating system nor Apple itself can access it. Those safeguards are reassuring on paper, though they aren’t something I could independently verify while testing a smart display in my kitchen.

Sources indicate that that reliance on a nearby iPhone or iPad is also the source of the HomeView’s most frustrating quirk. With my phone on me, Siri sometimes can’t decide which device should answer. The first few times I tried to set a simple timer, it turned into a dance between the HomeView and my phone before one of them finally took the request. It takes a little getting used to.

It has been revealed that your iPhone also supplies a massive share of the HomeView’s apps. There’s no App Store on the device. It ships with 15 built-in apps, including Safari, FaceTime, Music, and Home, and it pulls a handful of other Apple apps, like TV and News, from your phone. So, if you don’t mind some severe letterboxing, you can watch TV and movies on there. Supported third-party audio and video apps show up from a paired iPhone, too, through a system that works a lot like CarPlay. If a service you rely on doesn’t support it, there’s no way to install it on the HomeView directly.

In a recent development, the HomeView’s main job is running your smart home, and that’s where my experience was most mixed. It controls accessories you’ve added to Apple Home, which includes supported HomeKit and Matter devices. My Ring cameras don’t integrate with Apple Home natively, so they never appeared in the HomeView’s Home Camera face, which can otherwise show up to nine live feeds at once. It worked easily with my smart lighting and other natively compatible devices.

Check whether your current cameras, locks, sensors, and thermostat show up in Apple Home before you initiative to run the whole house from this screen. If they don’t, budget for HomeKit or Matter replacements that do (and Apple has a whole suite of upcoming options developed alongside LG and Schneider Electric).

According to recent reports, the actual smart hub interface that displays on screen is handy for keeping tabs on what’s going on in your home. It’s notable to note that this thing looks like a thermostat when it’s on the wall, but it isn’t one. Maybe a future model with a built-in thermostat could free up some wall space.

According to recent reports, the HomeView turned out to be a great cooking assistant. Once you open a recipe page on the web, either on your iPhone or in Safari on the HomeView, a Start Cooking button reformats it so you can follow the steps in real time while you work. Recipe pages vary wildly in how they’re formatted and coded, and I expected that mess to trip it up. It has worked without a problem every time I’ve used it so far.

I made a fairly simple recipe for peanut butter noodles, and the instructions and timers were helpful and easy to use. More complicated recipes are more of a challenge, especially since you can’t really perform more than one step at a time, so don’t expect it to turn you into Gordon Ramsay overnight.

According to recent reports, as for the audio, the tabletop HomeView sounds full for its size. Its base holds a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators, almost like a subwoofer in miniature (but without the extension), and the display adds two custom full-range down-firing drivers of its own. I’d been using an older Google smart display before this, and the jump in sound quality is obvious.

In separate tests, PopSci editor Tony Ware spent a couple of nights with his own HomeView and some of his favorite songs and came away with positive impressions. Compared to a HomePod mini, the beat hits more convincingly. While there’s not much room for excursion in the base, output manages to be surprisingly potent without sacrificing clarity. It won’t beat some recent whole-home audio-focused connected speakers (or Apple’s own full-sized 2nd-gen. HomePod, for that matter), but it’s plenty room-filling for such a compact, multipurpose enclosure. Whether you’re chopping carrots or choppin’ it up with friends, the HomeView is more than enough speaker for a smaller space.

In a recent development, what was more impressive was the airy, open presence of Dolby Atmos tracks from Apple Music, given the use of reflections and computational audio rather than an actual array of directional drivers. With accelerometers and Apple silicon adjusting the acoustic system’s EQ and output based on the screen’s tilt, the result is more incisive than immersive … how it will always be when you can’t surround yourself with speakers. Still, it projects clearly without sounding overly bright or edgy, which is good for podcasts to playlists.

Sources indicate that there are occasional kinks, however. If you’re into spatial audio, the best way to ensure you’re getting the correct version of a track is to ask the HomeView to pull Apple Music directly from the cloud; sometimes the Dolby Atmos badge won’t pop up when you send a track from your phone over AirPlay, so you can’t be certain it’s not just stereo. Alternatively, you can hand off whatever is playing on your phone by bringing it close enough to the HomeView to get an AirDrop ripple animation and the album art to show up. Also, you might find yourself instinctively running your finger along the edge of the display looking for volume buttons, but there are no physical controls, which isn’t surprising from an aesthetic standpoint but still feels like a shortcoming.

Industry observers note that the Apple HomeView makes the most sense on a nightstand, on the wall next to your thermostat, or in the kitchen. Its Photos face turns it into a digital picture frame, which keeps it from looking like a giant Apple Watch stuck to your wall or sitting on your table (though the clock faces are cute and colorful).

It has been revealed that if your home already runs on an iPhone and Apple Home accessories, HomeView slots right in and puts it all on one screen you’ll actually want to look at. If you’ve built your smart home around gear that doesn’t work with Apple Home, however, blueprint to replace it before you make the jump.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles. For context, that’s far enough to mow every inch of space between the Earth and Moon.

Greenzie declared the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.

And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the organization really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.

“We mowed to the moon, but the real achievement is the commercial experience behind those miles,” says Charles Brian Quinn, co-founder and CEO of Greenzie and almost definitely the guy who first came up with the lunar lawncare line. “Every mile represents equipment working on real properties with commercial crews. That experience has shaped our technology, strengthened our OEM partnerships and taught us how to help customers successfully integrate autonomy into their daily operations.”.

Recent findings suggest that greenzie develops autonomous packages for, and maintains OEM relationships with electric brands Mean Green Electric Mowers (whose Vanquish Autonomous commercial mower is shown, above), and Greenworks Commercial, as well as gas-powered brands like Bobcat and Wright Manufacturing. Regardless of what powers the mowers, Greenzie supplies the self-driving technology and integration expertise, while its OEM partners develop and manufacture the equipment that does the actual cutting, clearing, and whatever else their clients need.

“Successful autonomy requires more than capable technology,” noted Steve Bush, chief operating officer of Greenzie. “Customers need to understand where autonomy fits into their operations, how to prepare their crews and how to measure success. We have spent years learning those lessons alongside our customers and OEM partners, creating a more consistent path to adoption as the industry grows.”.

The Mean Green Vanquish Autonomous featured gere is a fully electric, stand-on, zero-turn (ZTR) mower built around an all-day-ready 22 kWh li-ion battery pack and featuring a 60″ rear-discharge mulching deck.

Mean Green claims that the combination of substantial battery and the electric motors that drive the ZTR mower and spin up its blades are good up to eight hours of continuous mowing on a charge, with an aluminum chassis and deck helping to keep the machine’s overall weight down for easier towing maximum efficiency.

The company indicates the mower can operate in either manual or autonomous mode, with Greenzie’s self-driving software supported by six depth-sensing stereo cameras providing 360-degree vision, RTK-corrected GPS, and visual-inertial odometry for onboard site mapping and precise positioning, which Greenzie says allows the mower to detect obstacles up to twenty feet away, recognize designated keep-out zones, and automatically return to its starting point when called back.

A top speed of 11.5 mph and the ability to repeat saved mowing routes, the Vanquish is designed to give commercial landscaping crews another productive worker without adding another person to the payroll … which, with a $60,000 asking price, is money they will probably still need.

Let’s get some pro-labor rage going in the comments, and don’t forget to mention what kind of paycheck you’d need to get to go work in landscaping 2,000+ hours a year while you’re there.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, airports can be a bit intimidating.
  • Industry observers note that and while I love a good matching sweatsuit as much as the next guy, there are plenty of other ways to dress comfortably for the airport.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, airports can be a bit intimidating. You’ve got the TSA line to worry about, but more importantly, you have your outfit to figure out. Unfortunately, some people judge what you’re wearing while traveling (it’s me, I’m people). But I also don’t think looking presentable has to be that hard. Some guys show up in full sweats, looking like they're about to spend the next six hours in bed. Others dress like they're heading straight from baggage claim to a dinner reservation. Personally, I think there's a happy medium somewhere in there. You should be comfortable enough to sleep through your flight, but you also shouldn't have to change your entire outfit the second you land. From comfortable pants and breathable T-shirts to stylish sneakers, these are the essentials worth packing for your next flight.

Industry observers note that and while I love a good matching sweatsuit as much as the next guy, there are plenty of other ways to dress comfortably for the airport. We’ve got stretchy trousers that look pretty darn good, a solid pair of sneakers, and layers that work alone or together. It's about finding clothes that do a little bit of everything, especially if you like to travel light.

If you’re looking to spruce up your fit for your next flight (and to become someone’s airport crush), here’s what to know.

I'm not saying you can't wear jeans on a plane, but why would you when you have so many more comfortable alternatives? You'll be sitting for hours, probably in a seat that doesn't give you much room to move, so the last thing you want is a waistband digging into your stomach. Look for pants with a little stretch, breathable fabrics, and a relaxed fit that won't feel restrictive when you're sitting down. Brands like Vuori and DUER have gotten particularly good at making pants that feel like loungewear without necessarily looking like it. And if you're committed to sweatpants, that's perfectly fine, too. Just go for a pair with a cleaner, more structured fit.

Reigning Champ Midweight Terry Relaxed Sweatpant.

Nike Club Open Hem Brushed Fleece Pants.

You really don't need to overthink your airport T-shirt. A good cotton tee will do just fine, especially if it's something you already wear regularly. Personally, I'd avoid anything too tight or made from a heavy fabric, since airports and airplanes can get surprisingly stuffy. A slightly relaxed fit gives you more room to move and makes layering easier, too. I tend to gravitate toward simple, solid-colored tees because they go with practically anything. Uniqlo's AIRism Cotton Oversized T-Shirt is a good example of something that's affordable, comfortable, and easy to dress up or down depending on what else you're wearing.

Mack Weldon Pima Long Sleeve T-Shirt.

Everlane The Essential Organic Crew.

Recent findings suggest that I don't care if you're flying to Miami in the middle of July; bring a sweatshirt. Airplane cabins have a habit of feeling like refrigerators, and I'd much rather have an extra layer than spend an entire flight shivering. A good crewneck or hoodie is probably all you need, preferably something soft that isn't too bulky to stuff into your bag when you're not wearing it. I'm partial to oversized sweatshirts for traveling, though you don't need to go so big that you're drowning in fabric. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that three years ago, Mercedes-Benz rolled out the first Level 3 autonomy system offered in the United States. That system is no longer available in the latest revision to the S-Class, with CTO Jörg Burzer calling it “early.” The brand still has advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) ambitions, though, and two latest major products are arriving for a few customers starting next year. Mercedes-Benz has announced plans to launch both hands-free highway driving and hands-on point-to-point navigation in 2027, part of a continuing partnership with (scandal-laden) semiconductor superpower Nvidia. The latter system is subscription-only, although pricing for that subscription has yet to be revealed.

Sources indicate that the hands-free system is limited to “eligible roads,” effectively making it a specialized feature for freeway use. It works up to 85 miles per hour, allowing a driver to take their hands off all inputs while the system handles highway driving and decision-making under the driver’s active supervision. Point-to-point navigation, on the other hand, is a hands-on system with more freedom. Like Tesla or Rivian’s similar offerings, it is intended to handle most of the workload of city driving and react in real time to the peculiarities of that task.

While both systems reach closer to true autonomous driving, their designation as SAE Level 2 systems mean that they are still nowhere near complete autonomy. That label means that they are meant to be seen as driver assistance systems only, leaving the person in the driver’s seat ultimately responsible for intervening before a problem occurs. The same is true of every autonomous solution presently on offer, including systems marketed as “Full Self-Driving” by Tesla.

Industry observers note that some California residents will receive the opportunity to try both systems starting in December; hands-free driving is expected to reach eligible cars more broadly in spring of 2027, while point-to-point navigation is made available nationwide at some point during the next year. Subscription pricing has not yet been unveiled, but brand representatives have suggested to Road & Track that it will be “competitive” with similar offerings from other automakers.

In a recent development, mercedes allowed outlets, including Road & Track, to test both systems in San Francisco ahead of the news. You can read more about how the upcoming ADAS offerings fared here.

Industry observers note that fred Smith's love of cars comes from his fascination with auto racing. Unfortunately, that passion led him to daily drive a high-mileage, first-year Porsche Panamera. He is still thinking about the last lap of the 2011 Indianapolis 500.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that in 2003, the basin was excavated as an extension of the Khor Kalba mangrove trees.
  • Industry observers note that “Our results show just how critical coastal wetlands can be to young green turtles,” Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for one group of young sea turtles, a protected wetland in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) proved a perfect oasis. A team tracking nine juvenile green turtles (Chelonia mydas) found they were spending over 80 percent of their time in the Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area, a human-made lagoon on the UAE’s Gulf of Oman coast. Large numbers of turtles are also found in this basin built beyond the salt-tolerant trees and shrubs along the coast. A study published today in the journal Aquatic Conservation details the findings.

Recent findings suggest that in 2003, the basin was excavated as an extension of the Khor Kalba mangrove trees. The resulting Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area has been recognized as a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention and as a Key Biodiversity Area since 2013.

Industry observers note that “Our results show just how critical coastal wetlands can be to young green turtles,” Dr. Owen Exeter, a study co-author and marine conservation ecologist from the University of Exeter, remarked in a statement. “The fact these turtles are using the artificial basin appears to be a happy accident, and an example of how wildlife can find a way in a world increasingly shaped by humans. However, without the natural mangroves connecting to this system, it’s unlikely that this would have occurred.

Recent findings suggest that according to the team, the floor of the basin is covered with algae, which likely means the turtles have enough food. A few sharks are making their way to this habitat.

The turtles are now also showing “strong reliance” in the man-made basin, with five times higher odds of being found there than in surrounding habitats.

While this spot can be a refuge, the natural mangrove channels also play a critical role in connecting the juvenile turtles (those with a shell less than 23 inches across) to the sea. These channels allow them to move with the tides and show the importance of protecting the entire ecosystem, not just parts of it.

“The government of Sharjah at the moment protects most of this area from building development, fishing and boating—preserving the last mangrove ecosystem on UAE’s east coast,” Exeter remarked. “Coastal wetlands are tropical nature hotspots, providing essential nursery and foraging habitats for species including sea turtles. Wetlands are among the most threatened ecosystems globally, so we urgently need to understand how key species use both modified and protected wetlands.”.

Sources indicate that while these findings are positive for the turtles living in the protected area, their life cycle depends on nesting beaches. Many of these beaches have already been lost to coastal development, and fishing, vessel traffic, and pollution affect the other nearby areas.

One of the turtles swam over 430 miles south to central Oman, highlighting the need for conservation management of these mobile species once they are old enough to leave critical wetland sites.

“Overall, our findings show that coastal wetlands, including engineered ones, can provide valuable habitat for juvenile turtles, provided they are designed for ecological connectivity and subsequent human pressures and threats are minimised,” concluded study co-author Brendan Whittington-Jones from the Sharjah Environment and Protected Areas Authority (EPAA) who led the study.

  • Recent findings suggest that that, of course, also means that the map has exposed a few balance complications with some of the game’s weapons and tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, arc Raiders has received a upcoming patch today that’s almost entirely dedicated to balance and economy tweaks. Patch 1.3.0 arrived earlier across all platforms, coming in at just under 1GB. This is an especially interesting patch because many of the changes it makes can be seen as a response to player behaviour on Stella Montis, the game’s latest map, which just joined the roster last week.

Stella Montis is available for players who’ve put in a decent number of rounds, and its close-quarters, enclosed environments have essentially turned it into the latest “PvP map”, where constant action can be found.

Recent findings suggest that that, of course, also means that the map has exposed a few balance complications with some of the game’s weapons and tools. Case in point: the Venator, a pistol that saw a lot of use recently. The weapon is especially powerful when fully-upgraded, something Arc Raiders developer Embark said pushed it beyond what had been originally intended.

In a recent development, in today’s enhancement, the Venator's fire rate is the thing getting hit the hardest, with each upgrade now offering slower gains to the weapon's rate-of-fire compared to the way things were. The weapon’s weight is also being increased to five from two.

It has been revealed that another powerful item players have been getting a lot of mileage out of recently has been the Deadline mine. Unlike the Venator, the Deadline is mainly a threat to Arc enemies, and it’s proven incredibly powerful against the largest and most fearsome, such as the Bastion, and Leaper. In fact, the mine was considered essential when taking down a Queen.

The patch vastly increases its purchase price, and makes it more difficult to craft by upping the amount each of its components requires. Perhaps the most effective nerf, however, is the reduction to the Deadline’s stock at traders from three to just one, which means you’re going to be seeing a lot less of it topside.

Industry observers note that beyond those specific changes, Embark has also tweaked explosive damage across the board. According to the developer, explosive damage was being applied to multiple parts at once, which trivialised some encounters.

This change mainly affects larger Arc units, such as the Bastion, allowing them to withstand more explosive damage before bits start coming off of them. The Hullcracker, one of the best explosive damage weapons, has also caught a nerf as part of that.

Recent findings suggest that check the official blog for the full change log for patch 1.3.0. If you’re just getting started with the hottest extraction shooter ever, our Arc Raiders tips offer plenty of help. You should also learn what all the different Map Conditions do in Arc Raiders, and how to best make use of each of them.

Hospital ratings have become an notable resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

On October 27, Healthgrades announced the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.

The annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

Upcoming research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

In a recent development, around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” remarked Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

The ability to make informed decisions about your health — and where to get care — is a cornerstone of self-advocacy, and we are proud to help make that information accessible to all patients.”.

Healthgrades identifies hospitals that deliver exceptional outcomes across common outpatient procedures and specialty conditions.

Finding high quality care is notable, particularly amid a growing gap between top-performing and one-star hospitals.

According to Healthgrades, from 2023 to 2025, if all hospitals had performed at the five-star level from 2023 to 2025:.

“One of the biggest challenges is balancing increasing patient needs with the resources available to healthcare professionals,” Biggers stated.

“Hospitals face workforce shortages, growing administrative responsibilities, financial pressures, and increasing complexity in patient care. Physicians and other healthcare professionals need adequate time and support not only to evaluate and treat patients, but also to communicate results, coordinate follow-up care, and address concerns that arise between visits,” she continued.

“When healthcare teams are adequately supported, they are better positioned to communicate effectively with patients, coordinate care, and address patients’ needs.”.

Biggers mentioned that ensuring equal access to quality healthcare is challenging because of factors such as:.

Hospital closures and reduced services make access even more difficult. Biggers identified a few possible solutions, such as expanding outpatient care, building community partnerships, using telehealth when appropriate, and improving coordination among healthcare providers.

Recent findings suggest that “Ultimately, providing high quality care requires more than clinical expertise. It requires healthcare systems to invest in their workforce, strengthen care coordination, and create environments where healthcare professionals have the resources they need to provide safe, effective, and patient-centered care,” Biggers mentioned.

“Equally notable, healthcare systems must ensure that patients have meaningful access to these services, regardless of where they live or their socioeconomic circumstances.”.

Healthgrades acknowledges hospitals that excel in three aspects of specialty care:.

Biggers said that outstanding hospitals recognize that high quality care extends beyond just treating an illness.

“It involves listening to patients, understanding their individual circumstances, and ensuring they feel respected, informed, and involved in their healthcare decisions,” she mentioned.

Patients want to find a hospital that excels in the procedures or health conditions relevant to them.

The recipients of the Specialty Excellence Awards are among the top 15% of hospitals specializing in these areas.

Healthgrades evaluated patient outcomes at roughly 4,500 hospitals across 31 common procedures and conditions to reach their decisions.

Among the list of Specialty Excellence Award recipients, Healthgrades also recognizes America’s 100 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for 11 specialty areas andAmerica’s 50 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for four specialty areas.

“An outstanding hospital prioritizes both patient care and the people delivering that care,” Biggers told Healthline.

“While clinical outcomes, patient safety, and access to evidence-based treatments are essential measures of quality, I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development,” she continued.

Healthgrades awards U.S. hospitals that excel at Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, andOutpatient Prostate Care.

Outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.

From 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.

“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers noted.

Sources indicate that “Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.

To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.

Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.

Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.

Recent findings suggest that surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong? Or is it?

After Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in October 2024, Brownlee (MKBHD) noted there was no way Tesla would deliver a Cybercab to a customer for $30,000 or less before 2027. If it did, he’d shave his head on camera.

Sources indicate that musk has taken it personally ever since. When the first Cybercab came off the Giga Texas line in February, he replied “Gonna happen 😂” to a bald-MKBHD meme, which we covered at the time. In September, after Brownlee doubled down in a latest video, Musk wrote: “I guess he really wants to shave his head 🤷‍♂️”.

According to recent reports, on Friday, Tesla started inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use. The order page lists $29,990, a mandatory $299 per month Autonomy Subscription, a $1,000 non-refundable deposit, and an estimated delivery of December 2026, only in Tesla’s Texas Robotaxi cities.

Recent findings suggest that as we reported Friday, the car only operates inside Tesla’s Robotaxi geofences. And Tesla’s Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement says it “will not operate” without the $299 initiative, bans owners from putting it on the Robotaxi network or using it for ride-hailing, and lets Tesla shrink the operating area at any time.

It has been revealed that so Tesla designed a robotaxi, then offered it to select private owners who aren’t allowed to use it as a taxi. Over five years, that’s $47,631 before insurance, registration, and charging. And you are limited to small geofenced areas. If you stop paying Tesla’s monthly fee, which it can change at all times, your cybercab becomes a paperweight.

It has been revealed that brownlee laid out his case Friday night. There are no deliveries yet, the car is invite-only rather than publicly available, and it can’t be used as a cab outside of the existing geofences. He called it “a paperweight if I take this thing home,” though he admits that last point isn’t technically part of the bet.

It has been revealed that the memes are everywhere, so let’s go back over the bet: Cybercab publicly available for under $30k by the end of 2026My hair is safe for several reasons1: No deliveries yet. But they’re estimating starting in December so that’s neat2: Invite only, not actually publicly… https://t.co/NCD2aFbe2c.

Tesla fans fired back with clips from his September video, where he described a car that “will not ship to regular people like you and me for $30k before the end of 2026.” Whole Mars Catalog, an Elon Musk propagandist whose real name is Omar Qazi, told him to “be a man and honor your word.” Musk reposted it, then replied:.

Musk also reposted a Grok answer claiming the current offer “matches” the conditions of the bet.

But around the same time, Musk replied directly to Brownlee’s post about the order page, and it didn’t help Tesla’s case:.

“It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”.

In a recent development, that’s Tesla’s CEO confirming, a day after launch, that the car can’t be sold outside the areas where it already operates and that its price is wrong. A price that Musk fully controls.

Sources indicate that yes, it looks like Tesla is rushing this out just to win a bet against a Youtuber. Absolutely insane behavior. We’ve seen this movie before. In June 2025, Tesla did a single “autonomous delivery” of a Model Y to meet a Musk deadline, then never did it again.

Tesla always pitched the Cybercab as a vehicle for its Robotaxi network. Now, seven weeks before the deadline, a personal-use version reveals up that’s invite-only, Texas-only, banned from doing the one thing it was designed for, and attached to a subscription Musk himself claims is too expensive. If you set out to build a product whose main job was letting Musk claim he won a Twitter bet, it would look a lot like this.

This Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it’s a permanent variable rate lease starting at $300 a month with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

Besides, the bet was "under 30k." Starting price is under 30k, but a subscription is required, which takes it over 30k, just to use it for one day. They could have given the car away for free, and just charged a fee to use it. Doesn't change the total cost.

Sources indicate that what do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

It has been revealed that you can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month. 8 Questions to Know If Your Relationship Is 'Fake Happy'

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (456 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Psychologytoday

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Relationships can be messy and complicated, yet they remain the most beautiful connections we can form.
  • Recent findings suggest that research is now unraveling why your authentic self is better than slapping on a fake smile, especially in your love life.
  • In a study that investigated individuals’ awareness and acceptance of mental health concerns, researchers explored the influence of toxic positivity—the societal pressure to pretend everything’s fine, even when it’s not—on well-being.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Relationships can be messy and complicated, yet they remain the most beautiful connections we can form. But what happens when a partner tells you to put on a happy face and to stay positive no matter what—suggesting that you sweep the mess under the rug? This is what psychologists refer to as “toxic positivity,” and it is more common in relationships than we’d like to admit, and detrimental, too.

Recent findings suggest that research is now unraveling why your authentic self is better than slapping on a fake smile, especially in your love life. In light of this, psychologists can now measure whether your relationship embraces authenticity.

In a study that investigated individuals’ awareness and acceptance of mental health concerns, researchers explored the influence of toxic positivity—the societal pressure to pretend everything’s fine, even when it’s not—on well-being. According to the authors, “When we force our brain to be in a false state of wellness, we send a message to our brain that whatever the emotion is, it is in some way bad or dangerous.”.

When we avoid emotional discomfort, we may unintentionally be making those feelings larger and more overwhelming in the back of our minds. Pushing down real emotions leaves a mark, and those feelings sneak up on you when you least expect. Avoiding emotional discomfort doesn’t make it disappear; it just amplifies it.

According to recent reports, relationships thrive on authenticity. Pretending everything’s perfect when it’s not can be like throwing fuel on the flames. Research consistently highlights that being open about your feelings is key to a healthy and stable love life.

In light of this, research in Personality and Individual Differences aided the development of the Authenticity in Relationships Scale, a tool that measures how true to yourself and others you are in your social connections. The scale includes eight items to which respondents rate their level of agreement:.

It has been revealed that researchers have concluded that real-life couples who toss aside the “fake it till you make it” script report more satisfaction and resilience when the going gets tough. The developers of the scale found authenticity to predict higher levels of agency and communion within relationships, as well as greater subjective well-being at the individual level.

Open conversations, mutual respect, and a team mindset should always be the goal. Inauthenticity or toxic positivity, on the other hand, makes for a relationship filled with eye-rolling at genuine concerns, brushing off real problems, or pretending everything is sunshine and rainbows when it’s not.

Relationships flourish when we acknowledge and respect emotions authentically.

#5427. Smartwatch blood pressure monitoring was okay. AI is making it better.
