EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Roadandtrack ↗ Open Full Page

The Electric BMW M3 Delivers Thrills, Synthesized Sounds, and Pretend Gears

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, attend an event organized by BMW’s M Division, and you know what you are going to get.
  • According to recent reports, but then, as the noise grew louder, the narrative shifted.
  • According to recent reports, we’ve known for some time that the BMW M3 was going to make the switch to becoming an EV, but the reality of what that entails for those watching from outside the car was still a mild shock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, attend an event organized by BMW’s M Division, and you know what you are going to get. Such as plentiful M branding everywhere. It was no surprise when I arrived at BMW’s proving ground in Miramar, France, to experience the M3 prototype for the first time to see numerous flags and banners with the famous slant “M” logo. And it felt equally natural for a moment to be listening to the sound of a hard-worked engine on the test track, with what seemed the entirely M-appropriate howl of a straight-six exhaling through a minimally muffled exhaust.

According to recent reports, but then, as the noise grew louder, the narrative shifted. Because it was an M4 GT4 making the compelling racket. The two M3 prototypes that followed it wearing a vibrant, dazzle pattern disguise, were traveling every bit as quickly but almost entirely silently.

According to recent reports, we’ve known for some time that the BMW M3 was going to make the switch to becoming an EV, but the reality of what that entails for those watching from outside the car was still a mild shock. The good news for anyone unsure about such a radical departure for the subbrand is that work on a gasoline-powered M3 is continuing in parallel. The combustion version, with the development code G85, is likely to feature another version of the S58 turbocharged inline-six from the current G80 generation, likely working in conjunction with some level of hybrid assistance. That will be a much more traditional take on the junior M car, but it almost certainly won’t be as powerful or as quick as the fully electric version.

But is our world ready for this level of different?

My first experience at Miramar was a passenger ride around the handling track, sitting in the left seat of one of the four colorfully-wrapped prototypes beside Sven Esch, M’s head of vehicle dynamics. I knew the car had a quad-motor powertrain, with one motor driving each wheel, and I could see it was riding on new Michelin Pilot Sport S 6 tires, but that was about all I had to go on when Esch executed a full launch-control start, one brutal enough to leave me confident the finished car will be another member of the two-second club when it comes to 0–60 times. The other disclosure, delivered from the changing tone of the noise coming from the speakers and the sight of Esch’s fingers working paddles behind the steering wheel, is that BMW is joining Hyundai, Porsche, and Mercedes in having a simulated gear system. The lap also revealed a handling balance familiar from many generations of M cars, with varying angles of oversteer through most of the corners.

Sources indicate that there are still many unknowns. Although the cars at Miramar were close to production spec, BMW is keeping many details to itself. There are no performance claims yet. And every number given for power, torque, range and charging speed carried an asterisk leading to an “approximately” proviso. The maximum system output was quoted at 838 hp and 885 lb-ft, with the pair of front motors able to deliver up to 643 hp and 398 lb-ft working together, while the larger two in back max out at a claimed 750 hp and 738 lb-ft. Given the way automotive PR typically works, I would be surprised if any of those figures grew any worse before becoming finalized. But they are clearly a way off the 1153-hp AMG GT 63 4-Door, the 1123-hp Lucid Air Sapphire, and the 1019-hp Porsche Taycan Turbo GT.

In a recent development, the M3 EV uses a different battery pack from the regular i3, with a fresh cell design and double-sided cooling to enable huge peak flow rates, with this having approximately 100 kWh of usable energy and operating at up to 800 volts. BMW is predicting an EPA range of 300 miles, and peak DC charging speeds will be around 420 kilowatts—slightly higher than the regular i3 and better than the speediest Taycan, but a way off the 600-kW capability of the AMG. More impressive is the ability of the battery pack to reabsorb energy through regeneration, doing this at rates of up to—approximately again—540 kilowatts. So the equivalent of 724 hp, without having to use the carbon-ceramic discs and pads.

Then there are the simulated gears. Although, pedantically, these are not. BMW has decided the mDrive mode allows the selection of what it calls “stages,” of which there are six. The default mode on startup is actually Automatic, in which the car changes between the stages by itself while playing a corresponding soundtrack as it does so, like a true automatic transmission in drive. There is also a paddle mode that gives you the ability to select a stage and also a simulated limiter if you fail to change up in time. It also has a normal EV single-speed drive mode.

It has been revealed that beneath the surface, the M3 has been given a substantial structural work over compared with the i3, the M version getting additional reinforcement for suspension subframes and also plates that bolt to the underfloor battery pack front and rear to better integrate this into the car’s structure. There is also a strut brace between the front suspension towers, eliminating the i3’s frunk, plus smaller reinforcement struts within the A-pillars and on the rear towers.

According to recent reports, while the M3 might be beaten by rivals on power statistics, it turns tables with the complexity of its powertrain. Having individual motors for each wheel is a segment first, in contrast with the two-motor Taycan Turbo GT and the three-motor AMG GT 4-Door and Lucid Air Sapphire. The lack of any physical connection between the different wheels means all the functions normally handled by differentials and clutch packs have to be done electronically, a hugely complex task for the dynamic control system. But it also brings benefits, most obvious is the ability to vary the torque going to each individual wheel almost instantly, without the response delay of even the fastest-acting mechanical systems. And it can also do this with regeneration, changing the braking effect on each wheel with equal dexterity.

It has been revealed that my chance to experience all this witchcraft was limited to two stints on the Miramar handling track, following the raucous M4 GTS being piloted by works driver Jens Klingmann at a pretty gentle pace, and with Carsten Wolf, vehicle characteristics manager, riding shotgun. Wolf proved to be a pretty laid-back passenger, but I was only able to switch certain dynamic settings.

It has been revealed that while the electric M3’s cabin architecture is very similar to that of the i3 and the newly introduced 3-series, the prototype wore a dashboard cover to obscure what I’m told were unfinished screen-layout designs. The car did have an M-specific version of BMW’s Panoramic Vision extra-long gauge cluster, which features a rendered “rev counter” very similar in design to the one in the new M350 xDrive, two graphic bars moving apart. There was also a small set of color-changing shift lights.

It was immediately clear that performance was on another level to the i3 50 I had driven earlier the same day. The M3 felt every bit as quick as the power figures suggested it should, with none of the shortish straights of the handling track being long enough to bring any sense of acceleration beginning to tail off, even as speeds headed well north of 100 mph, and the M4 GT4 was visibly having to work hard to keep a gap. In a straightline fight, I’m certain the EV would have been the faster car, although riding on Pirelli slicks, and having Klingmann at the wheel, gave the car a clear advantage in corners.

Sources indicate that the M3’s steering was heavier than the i3 and M350’s and brought a far better sense of connection to the front tires. Unlike some cars with lots of electrical power going through the front axle, the prototype didn’t suffer from any steering corruption, albeit over what was generally a smooth track surface. Even in the softest Comfort mode, the car turned into corners with a keenness that was clearly being helped by applying different levels of regen to each wheel, which then kept it locked to a chosen line.

Or at least, it stayed locked until I started to try and get early onto the accelerator. At which point a new sensation arrived, unexpected in an M3: mild understeer. The control systems were clearly intervening hard in the background; winding off lock brought full fury back immediately. At Wolf’s suggestion, I pressed the steering wheel’s M1 button to shift the drivetrain and chassis to their Sport setting, reducing the front-end push.

But it required the M2 button, which brought the most aggressive Sport Plus settings, and putting the stability control into its half-off MDM mode to unlock the M3’s party spirit and show the side of its personality I’d first experienced from the passenger’s seat, with progressive, easily controllable oversteer.

Plenty of magic was still going on behind the scenes. I noticed that even if I wasn’t quick to apply opposite lock, the prototype would still hold a tidy drift, the dynamic brain carefully metering the torque going to each corner—I was in no doubt that turning the stability management fully off would be a different level of challenge. But, at last, the M3 was feeling like an M3 should.

The wheel-by-wheel regeneration was much more subtle. The i3 already blends electrical and friction braking seamlessly, and the M3 is on a different level, able to use regen to the point of ABS intervention. The left pedal was firm and proportionate, and I had no sense of when one side was handing over to the other. But even under track loadings, most slowing was being done electrically. At the end of my first stint, Wolf, smiling, handed me an infrared temperature reader and invited me to measure the brake temperatures. At the front, the carbon disc was at just 100 degrees Celsius (212 degrees Fahrenheit), way less than I would expect after 10 minutes of track driving in an 800-hp car that weighs around 5000 pounds. The other advantage of the ability to harvest so much energy is a significant improvement to track range; Wolf notes that for every three laps the car was recuperating enough for another lap at the same pace.

What about the virtual gears? Sorry, the “stages.” These were less convincing. The sounds being piped over the M3’s speakers are loud and engine-like, especially at lower simulated revs, but they grow more otherworldly and sci-fi as the shift lights start to illuminate: I was detecting distinct notes of TIE fighter. M has deliberately taken a different direction from AMG, which has the GT 4-dr doing a full-fledged V-8 impression. BMW’s approach is arguably the more honest one; the M3 isn’t pretending to be something it isn’t.

It has been revealed that but I noticed that the stages also had much less torque modeling than rivals such as Porsche’s E-Shift system in the Taycan, or the pioneering e-Shift in the Hyundai Ioniq 5N, which started this whole game. Beyond the possibility of hitting the M3’s artificial limiter, being in the wrong gear didn’t bring much obvious penalty on track. After a couple of laps of changing with the paddles, I actually went back to Automatic mode, where the virtual gears shift themselves. Which proved that the rising and falling soundtrack does help orientate corner entry speeds. Driving the slow-down lap with both the stepped gears and the speed sound turned off made the M3 prototype suddenly feel like a sensory deprivation chamber.

Sources indicate that what was a very limited first drive was clearly aimed at raising anticipation for the finished car more than answering every dynamic question. It was enough to prove that this M3 is a radical shift from its predecessors. But also to validate BMW’s claim that it is set to be the fastest and most powerful M car yet. The prototype also felt at home on a racetrack in a way that EVs very rarely do, and it has clearly been designed with circuit work in mind. This is a very, very different M3—and I’m glad there will still be a more traditional one. But the electric version still feels worthy of its famous badge.

Industry News: Can squirrels really survive any fall?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on any ordinary day, you might witness the breathtaking display of squirrels high in the trees, doing what seems like effortless, daredevilish parkour.
  • A large, heavy human being attempting these same maneuvers would likely fall—and would be looking at a trip to the E.R., at best.
  • Yet squirrels, it seems, tend to walk away from these situations unscathed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on any ordinary day, you might witness the breathtaking display of squirrels high in the trees, doing what seems like effortless, daredevilish parkour. They might launch themselves off one branch, bounce off another, and somehow reorient themselves in midair like it’s nothing.

A large, heavy human being attempting these same maneuvers would likely fall—and would be looking at a trip to the E.R., at best.

Yet squirrels, it seems, tend to walk away from these situations unscathed. You’ve probably even heard that squirrels can survive a fall from any height. But according to Dr. Nathaniel Hunt of the University of Nebraska at Omaha, this comes with an key caveat: Even these brazen little gymnasts don’t stick the landing every single time.

According to recent reports, “I would put an asterisk on the claim that squirrels can survive a fall from literally any height,” Hunt tells Popular Science. “Their size makes large falls surprisingly survivable, but they are not invulnerable.”.

So, can squirrels survive, if not all, most falls? And if so, how?

Industry observers note that it’s much more than luck that keeps squirrels landing safely; they are no more immune than we are to the laws of gravity. It’s what happens in the air—both in terms of their anatomical engineering and their instincts—that allows them to survive most falls and get right back to their nut-hiding hijinks.

According to Hunt, a falling squirrel faces three challenges: the speed of the fall, its orientation midair, and the impact when it lands. A squirrel’s small body helps; at about a pound, a squirrel weighs about as much as a loaf of bread.

In a recent development, “Being small gives it a lot of aerodynamic area relative to its weight, so air resistance limits its speed,” Hunt claims. “It also has much less kinetic energy than a larger animal.”.

In a recent development, so, squirrels’ light and small bodies help them hit the ground with less force, but that’s not all that’s going on. Hunt says squirrels instinctively know how to move through the air and land on the ground, which helps to optimize their already “favorable physics.” The tail is a key player in these midair maneuvers.

“The tail is more interesting than a fluffy parachute,” Hunt notes. “At low airspeeds, aerodynamic forces are small, but the squirrel can still use inertial tail movements to exchange angular momentum with the body and control orientation.” In other words, squirrels use their tail to control how and where they fall.

Research backs Hunt’s claim. A 2021 study found that squirrels experiencing unexpected falls were able to rapidly rotate their tails, a motion that caused the rest of their bodies to rotate in the opposite direction. Hunt compared the role of the tail to that of a “reaction wheel” on a spacecraft.

“Accelerating the tail in one direction helps rotate or stabilize the body in the other direction,” Hunt notes.

Recent findings suggest that as a squirrel’s fall picks up speed, the tail may function more like the feathers on an arrow, Hunt suggests. If the squirrel starts to veer off course, the airflow pushes against the tail just enough to redirect its body into a stable position. Even then, the tail isn’t acting like a true parachute; instead of slowing the squirrel’s descent, the tail is nudging its body in the right direction.

It has been revealed that size, anatomy, and aerial reorientation are all important to a squirrel’s seemingly magical ability to survive most falls. However, there’s a third skill that plays an equally important part, one Hunt thinks may be “the most underappreciated part of the story.” Squirrels know how to come in for a landing.

It has been revealed that “A recent study I co-authored found that fox squirrels managed more than 80 percent of their landing energy through their forelimbs,” Hunt claims of a study looking at squirrels leaping between branches. “They also adjusted their forces depending on whether they undershot or overshot the branch.”.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, a landing isn’t just something that happens to a squirrel. On some level, they’re doing damage control.

According to recent reports, “They are not simply hitting the branch,” Hunt states. “They are actively controlling the collision.”.

So, how slowly does a squirrel have to fall to be able to walk away?

The answer lies in our furry friend’s terminal velocity, the top speed something reaches while falling once air resistance balances gravity’s pull and stops it from accelerating further. Hunt notes a squirrel’s terminal velocity can be reasonably estimated at about 20 to 40 mph, depending on its posture, limb position, and tail. For reference, Hunt estimates the terminal velocity of a cat—famous nine lives aside—at about 60 mph, while a belly-down human skydiver is likely to fall at about 120 mph.

“All of these are approximate, because posture matters enormously,” he indicates.

According to recent reports, posture explains some of the variation, but size is ultimately the main driver. A giant squirrel, therefore, would likely fare much worse in a fall, even with perfect tail control and posture.

“You could not simply build a squirrel 10 times larger and expect it to tolerate the same fall,” Hunt notes.

In a recent development, likewise, a squirrel’s comparatively slow terminal velocity doesn’t mean it’s out of the proverbial woods. It might seem that once a squirrel hits its maximum speed, height wouldn’t matter much, making a fall from 10 feet and a fall from 100 feet equally survivable. Hunt cautions against assumptions like this.

“Reaching terminal velocity does not make a squirrel immune to injury,” he indicates. “The landing surface, body orientation, and any collisions along the way still matter.”.

This complex interplay of physics, instinct, learning, and split-second decision-making is part of what makes squirrels a fascinating study subject for Hunt.

It has been revealed that “What fascinates me is that you cannot neatly separate ‘the brain’ from ‘the mechanics,'” Hunt claims. “Squirrel agility emerges from sensing, learning, body shape, and physical dynamics working together.”.

Worried About Your Drinking? How to Cut Down, Comfortably

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1252 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Sources indicate that how is your relationship with alcohol?
  • Alcohol is ubiquitous and hard to consume healthily, even with the best of intentions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Sources indicate that how is your relationship with alcohol? Do you feel like you drink too much, perhaps vowing to cut down but slipping back into uncomfortable but familiar patterns? Many of us do. And that's hard, because alcohol is a socially acceptable drug, especially in Western societies. In the UK, you can buy it in supermarkets, grocery shops on every corner, in pubs, restaurants, and cafés. If you go to a party, alcohol is served. Or at dinner, people keep topping up your glass.

Alcohol is ubiquitous and hard to consume healthily, even with the best of intentions. Even if you're not alcohol-dependent, you may be uncomfortable about the amount you consume, but feel powerless to change that. Unfortunately, numerous studies show that regular drinking can have a major impact on your health, contributing to diseases including cancer, cardiovascular disease, dementia, and gastrointestinal diseases. It's clear that, in an ideal world, sobriety is the healthiest choice we can make. And if you do enjoy a glass of wine or beer, drinking in moderation is the next best option.

If you would like to cut down, the first step is to understand why you drink too much. Let's start with the fact that alcohol tastes and feels good. If you've had a long day, a glass or two of wine helps you relax, gives you a warm, fuzzy feeling, and helps you transition from work to downtime. These transitions can be tricky for us, and we may use substances to help—for example, the morning coffee that provides the energy boost we need to transition from sleepiness to an alert, ready-to-work mode.

In a recent development, so, like other oft-consumed substances, alcohol feels good and helps us transition from one state to another. Another factor in our alcohol consumption is peer pressure. In my country, this starts as a teenager, when friends encourage you to drink excessively to be "cool" or "fun." This pressure continues at university, where heavy drinking is often socially sanctioned and encouraged.

Even in middle age and later years, having a beer in pubs or half a bottle of wine with dinner is seen as normal and desirable. Opting not to drink, although more and more common, can be tricky if your friends are on the boozier side. Although sobriety is increasingly embraced by the younger generation, people of my age (approaching 60) have grown up with alcohol, and opting for sobriety, or occasional drinking, is an effortful, often socially frowned-upon choice.

Industry observers note that viewed through an internal family systems (IFS) lens, there is another pressure to drink, coming from inside your head. In IFS, drinking to excess, or in any way compulsively, is due to the actions of a protective part known as a "firefighter." This part's sole purpose is to extinguish the flames of pain that another—young, vulnerable—part might be struggling with. Firefighters are reactive and impulsive and have no sense of consequences—if you drink a whole bottle of wine, you may feel awful in the morning, but if it helps you feel less stressed, anxious, or lonely in the moment, the part's work is done.

Sources indicate that although the strategy of these firefighting parts can be terrible (they are also the parts that get people addicted to opioids, use pornography, gamble, and do all kinds of risky, self-destructive behaviour), they mean well. This cycle—a hurt, young part getting triggered and a protector urgently getting rid of the pain—is called an "addictive process" in IFS. And the same basic process applies, whether you are using substances or activities to numb, avoid, or distract yourself from painful feelings.

This can be hard to understand, so let's use Grace* as an example. Grace was a middle-aged white woman who came to see me for help with her drinking. She was a successful marketing executive with a young family, so she could ill afford the regular hangovers that blighted her life. "Every Monday morning I wake up with a pounding headache and a cold sweat," she told me in our first session. "I always overdo it on Sunday nights, because I'm so stressed out about going back to work. Then it's a bottle or more of wine, which helps me de-stress but of course makes the next day a nightmare.".

In a recent development, one of our early tasks was to translate Grace's suffering into parts language. I explained that she had a young part, Little Grace, who found her high-pressure job extremely stressful. We later learned that it also triggered memories of being under intense pressure from her high-flying, academic parents, making school and exams hellish for her. When this stressed little girl got triggered by the mammoth to-do list waiting for her on Monday morning, a firefighter stepped in to wash away all that stress with way too much Chardonnay.

Industry observers note that one of the many ways in which IFS requires a paradigm shift from other therapies is that, in order to help Grace drink in moderation, we had to work with the wine-drinking firefighter, not try to get rid of it (the well-meaning approach of 12-step programmes). When I spoke to this part, I learned that it had developed when Grace was a child, getting her to eat sweets and zone out in front of the TV after a day of grinding through her studies, while Grace's parents criticised her harshly for any mistakes. This revealed us that, like all protective parts, this one meant well, even if it was causing chaos in her life.

It has been revealed that we got permission from the firefighter to help Little Grace, which we did using IFS's "healing steps"—a roadmap for connecting with, comforting, and ultimately healing hurt young parts like this. We transported her from the past to live with adult Grace in the present, joining her loving, rambunctious family, which made her very happy. Only then could we work with the firefighter on changing their approach, which they gladly did. After much debate about becoming entirely sober or cutting down, Grace chose the latter, so we came up with a strategy to only drink on Friday and Saturday with dinner, and nothing on Sunday or during the week.

In a recent development, because all her parts had bought into this strategy, Grace could stick to it with relative ease, unlike the get sober/relapse/get sober again cycle common to many models for treating addiction. She ended therapy feeling optimistic about her future and with all the skills she needed to keep checking in on both Little Grace and the drinking part, to make sure they were OK, especially when she had a wobble and felt like slipping back into her old patterns.

Sources indicate that I hope that's helpful for you. If you are struggling with your drinking, or any other substance/activity that feels compulsive for you, please do seek help. It's always possible to heal early wounds and change these painkilling habits, so don't suffer in silence—life is too short to waste feeling bad about yourself and your choices.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

#5366. Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1760 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1760 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety.
  • But that simple statement also hides something key.
  • Sources indicate that not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety. Motorcycles are dangerous. All the statistics point to the fact that per mile, motorcycles are significantly more dangerous. And as someone who promotes them as a better alternative to large cars and trucks for many trips, it’s an uncomfortable reality that must be grappled with.

But that simple statement also hides something key. Not all motorcycles, riders, or riding behaviors carry the same risk. And as a latest generation of smaller electric motorcycles begins to emerge, I think there’s an interesting question worth asking: Could electric motorcycles inadvertently make motorcycling safer?

Sources indicate that not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline. It isn’t. Rather, because electrification may fundamentally change the type of motorcycle that hits the road.

In 2024, 6,228 motorcyclists were killed in the US, accounting for 16% of all traffic fatalities, according to the NHTSA.

Obviously, motorcycles have a fundamental disadvantage here. You don’t have a steel cage around you. There aren’t crumple zones separating your body from an oncoming SUV. There’s no seatbelt holding you in place or curtain airbag waiting to catch your head.

But there’s another component to motorcycle fatalities that is harder to ignore: rider behavior.

Industry observers note that around 35% of motorcyclist deaths in 2024 occurred in single-vehicle crashes, according to the IIHS. In other words, more than one-third of those deaths didn’t involve a rider being hit by another vehicle. At that point, whether or not a crash occurred was essentially in the hands of the rider.

Alcohol is another major factor. Among riders killed in single-vehicle crashes, the NHTSA reports that 40% were alcohol-impaired.

Then there are the bikes themselves.

In a recent development, supersport motorcycles stand out for all the wrong reasons. Of the riders killed on supersports in 2024, 59% were under 30. Compare that to cruiser and standard motorcycles, where just 19% of killed riders were under 30, or touring motorcycles at only 7%.

Sources indicate that that’s not proof that powerful motorcycles are causing those deaths, of course. There are all sorts of confounding factors, including the type of person attracted to different motorcycles and how those motorcycles tend to be ridden.

But it’s hard to ignore the broader picture.

To put it more plainly, a huge portion of motorcycle deaths are caused by riders simply going too fast, doing something wrong (like drinking or taking turns too aggressively), or because they couldn’t handle the power of an insanely high-performance crotch rocket. So while figures such as “motorcycles are 27x more deadly than cars” might be true in a broad sense, that doesn’t mean you have a 27x higher chance of death – especially not if you aren’t a 25-year-old hooligan on a second-hand liter bike.

One of the strange things about motorcycling is just how cheaply you can buy extraordinary performance.

Industry observers note that someone with relatively little riding experience can buy a used supersport capable of acceleration that would have required an exotic supercar not long ago. The motorcycle may weigh around 400 lb, produce well over 100 horsepower, and be capable of speeds approaching three times a typical US highway speed limit.

And unlike cars, there isn’t much protecting you when that performance gets away from you.

That’s why I find the current evolution of electric motorcycles so interesting.

For years, electric motorcycle companies largely chased gasoline motorcycles up the performance ladder. We got incredibly fast and powerful machines from companies like Energica and LiveWire.

Those bikes proved electric motorcycles could be fast.

But I’m increasingly interested in the opposite end of the spectrum.

Look at motorcycles such as LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho.

In a recent development, this isn’t an electric superbike designed around insane acceleration or a 150 mph (240 km/h) top speed. It’s a smaller motorcycle intended to offer approachable performance at a more accessible price.

It adds to a growing market already populated by highly acclaimed modest-sized electric motorcycles like those from Ryvid, Land, and Maeving.

And we’re seeing more machines begin to occupy this previously neglected territory between an e-bike and a full-size motorcycle.

That could make a huge difference when it comes to overall safety, as crotch rockets get replaced by sensible electric motorbikes.

In a recent development, battery technology actually creates an interesting incentive here. Making an electric motorcycle ridiculously powerful is easy. Giving it enough battery to sustain high speeds for long distances without becoming extremely heavy and expensive is much, much harder.

So the economics and physics of batteries naturally make smaller urban and suburban motorcycles fairly compelling right now.

Instead of asking how to build another 150 mph (240 km/h) electric motorcycle, manufacturers can build a lighter machine that goes 60 or 70 mph (95-120 km/h), has enough range for everyday riding, and costs considerably less.

Ironically, one of the limitations most commonly leveled against electric motorcycles could turn out to have a safety upside.

This is where I think things get even more interesting.

Sources indicate that for decades, the stereotypical progression into motorcycling might have involved learning on a dirt bike or small displacement motorcycle, then moving fairly promptly into larger machines. Often though, new riders simply took a licensing course and then bought their first 600cc sport bike to learn to ride.

But now we’re raising an entirely fresh generation on electric two-wheelers.

It has been revealed that kids and teenagers are increasingly growing up riding e-bikes and small electric motos. Eventually, many of them are going to want something faster than a 20 or 28 mph e-bike.

It has been revealed that A 50 mph (80 km/h) electric motorcycle is a pretty logical next step for the e-moto kids of today. Eventually, perhaps that rider graduates to something capable of 70 or 80 mph (120-130 km/h) and comfortable highway travel.

That’s a much more gradual performance curve than jumping from essentially no powered two-wheeler experience to a screaming 600cc supersport.

Industry observers note that there’s another advantage too: electric motorcycles are mechanically easier to operate. There’s generally no clutch, no gearbox, and no concern about stalling. Twist the throttle and go.

That doesn’t necessarily make them safer – instant electric torque can certainly get an inexperienced rider into trouble – but it does remove several tasks from the mental workload of learning to ride.

According to recent reports, the rider can spend more attention on braking, cornering, traffic, positioning, and the thousand other things that actually keep you alive on a motorcycle. The reduction in cognitive load can mean more focus on control, if it’s used that way.

To be clear, I’m not arguing that electric motorcycles are inherently safe.

They’re still motorcycles and they still lack cages. Well, most of them.

If an inattentive driver turns left in front of you, the chemistry powering your rear wheel isn’t going to make much difference.

It has been revealed that and electric motorcycles can be outrageously powerful. In fact, the instantaneous torque of an electric motor can make poor throttle calibration especially unforgiving for inexperienced riders.

There also simply isn’t enough data yet to demonstrate that electric motorcycles have meaningfully lower fatality rates than comparable gasoline motorcycles.

But that’s not really my argument.

Sources indicate that my argument is that electrification may change what we consider a normal beginner motorcycle. And that could be much more important, helping to significantly reduce accidents and deaths.

Recent findings suggest that I’m never going to pretend motorcycles can become as safe as cars. The physics simply don’t work that way.

But the broad statistic of “motorcycles are dangerous” encompasses an enormous spectrum of machines and riders.

A sober, trained commuter wearing proper protective gear and riding a modestly powered motorcycle to work is doing something fundamentally different from an inexperienced 21-year-old seeing how fast his supersport can take an empty freeway ramp at 2 a.m.

Yet both contribute to the same broad motorcycle fatality statistics.

In a recent development, what excites me about this emerging generation of electric motorcycles isn’t that swapping gasoline for batteries magically fixes motorcycle safety. It obviously doesn’t.

I bought a motorcycle around age 60 after considering the risk factors I could control:.

Industry observers note that I took a MSF basic riding course before buying the motorcycle. Best investment in the whole saga.

I never rode impaired. That was easy.

Industry observers note that I always rode with full protection. That was doable but inconvenient and seriously uncomfortable in hot weather.

It has been revealed that I never rode in rainy weather or at night. Again possible but limited my use of the motorcycle for commuting. Eventually my schedule changed to evening and stopped my motorcycle commuting altogether.

It has been revealed that after a few close calls I started avoiding roads with more than one lane in each direction. That added quite a bit to my commute time.

I never rode when I was in a hurry. That meant more days I didn't use the motorcycle for commuting.

None of these precautions have anything to do with electric drive. After I sold my gas motorcycle I test rode an electric motorcycle and loved it. However I didn't buy it because it didn't reduce any of the risks and I wouldn't ride it more than the gas bike.

It’s that electrification could help create a latest category of desirable, affordable motorcycles that don’t need 120 horsepower and a 160 mph top speed to be cool.

If younger riders grow up progressing from e-bikes to small e-motos and then to highway-capable electric motorcycles, perhaps we’ll wind up with a generation that sees a lightweight 60 or 70 mph motorcycle as a perfectly legitimate machine rather than merely a stepping stone to something ridiculously powerful.

Maybe electrification’s biggest contribution to motorcycle safety won’t be traction control, ABS, or sophisticated electronics.

Maybe it’ll simply make sensible motorcycles fun and cool again.

  • The patch is fairly small, and surprisingly doesn’t include any buffs or nerfs to anything in particular.
  • It has been revealed that the list of notes for upgrade 1.4.0 is compact, with a clear focus on addressing several exploits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh Arc Raiders patch has arrived, bringing a host of new fixes to several exploits players have recently been relying on to do things they’re not supposed to, and bypass certain mechanics to get into areas without having to go through proper channels.

The patch is fairly small, and surprisingly doesn’t include any buffs or nerfs to anything in particular.

It has been revealed that the list of notes for upgrade 1.4.0 is compact, with a clear focus on addressing several exploits. The biggest one, of course, is the addition of “exploit mitigation mechanisms” to stop players from glitching through locked doors.

In a recent development, this fix applies to all maps, and it’s intended to address an issue whereby players would not bring the required keys to access those areas of the various maps. Locked rooms, if they can be unlocked, often hide a wealth of high-tier and rare loot.

But players have also been using similar exploits to clip through walls and access areas outside the playspace, allowing them to ambush enemy players and set up traps that would be impossible for others to detect.

It has been revealed that the game’s recent patch, which was released exactly one week ago, mainly consisted of balance tweaks to some of the more popular weapons and mines. However, it also introduced a few fixes to prevent players from clipping through walls by using barricades.

While on the subject of being in places where you’re not supposed to, the patch blocked exterior access to the locked room inside Spaceport's Control Tower, making it only accessible from inside the tower.

Recent findings suggest that 1.4.0 also fixes an especially nasty exploit that allowed players to bring up their weapons much faster than normal by rapidly swapping to the quick use menu. There’s a range of smaller fixes for lighting and texture bugs here, too, and you can read all about it in the full change log below:.

Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember.
  • Industry observers note that we moved on to B.J.
  • We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

Industry observers note that we moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”.

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are at the moment midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

Recent findings suggest that for all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

In a recent development, for me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — also carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

Recent findings suggest that A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

Recent findings suggest that the research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

#5363. The Healthiest Thing You Can Do for Your Prostate at Age 50

The Healthiest Thing You Can Do for Your Prostate at Age 50

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in men, so you’d think doctors would be adamant about screening guys for it.
  • In a recent development, many guys didn’t know whether they should get it or not.
  • The American Cancer Society just came out with new guidelines that for the first time, unequivocally say that men should get the screening test.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in men, so you’d think doctors would be adamant about screening guys for it. Yet for years, prostate cancer screening via the PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test has been plagued by vague recommendations, and some back-and-forth messaging that flipped between “get it” and “the benefits might not be worth it.” Until recently, organizations including the American Cancer Society (ACS) used to give a recommendation that at age 50, guys should talk with their doctors about screening, then engage in a process of “shared decision-making” about whether to get the test.

In a recent development, many guys didn’t know whether they should get it or not. Without a clear recommendation, it was easy for some to think this PSA blood test wasn’t very important to do at all. The landscape has changed.

The American Cancer Society just came out with new guidelines that for the first time, unequivocally say that men should get the screening test. Guys at average risk should start at age 50. Guys at higher risk (more on that later) should start at 45.

Why that’s a big deal: “The new guideline not only gets rid of shared decision-making, which is really difficult to execute, is subject to bias, and is really time-intensive,” indicates Yaw Nyame, MD, of the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center at the University of Washington Medical Center. “But it couples that with a better understanding of what present-day prostate cancer screening is.”.

Today, the PSA test is “just the first step, not the final answer,” notes William Dahut, MD, chief scientific officer at ACS, and a contributing author to the guidelines. “It is a simple blood test, and an elevated result does not automatically mean cancer of the need for a biopsy.” Many more tools including MRIs and biomarkers help physicians drill down on who needs additional testing. “Our goal is to find prostate cancer earlier, while avoiding unnecessary procedures and treatment,” Dr. Dahut adds.

Industry observers note that what changed that prompted the revised recommendations? “It’s important to understand that guidance evolves as the evidence does,” claims Dr. Dahut. Research has piled up to indicate that PSA screening reduces prostate cancer deaths.

Recent findings suggest that “We do not need to make a disclaimer that maybe you should, maybe you shouldn’t do it. Everyone should do it and you should start early, especially if you have a higher risk of cancer,” says Dr. Nyame, who was on the expert panel that reviewed the new ACS screening guidelines.

While all men should get the test, according to the new guidelines, it’s not a “one size fits all” screening recommendation, Dr. Nyame explains. Recommendations vary according to risk. Find your category and screen according to that.

These are the new ACS guidelines for who and when:.

Other prostate screening guidelines came out earlier in 2026 from the American Urological Association (AUA) and the Society for Urologic Oncology (SUO) that had slightly different recommendations for the age at which you should start screening. What gives? The difference in recommended age and frequency of screening “has to do with how the guideline creators are viewing the different studies that they’re using to support their decision making,” Dr. Nyame notes.

Industry observers note that it doesn’t mean guys should throw up their hands and do nothing in frustration. “The AUA/SUO and ACS guidelines recognize the benefit of knowing a PSA test result earlier in life. A PSA test in the 40- to 50-year age range is a good predictor of the likelihood someone has or will develop a clinically significant prostate cancer,” notes James A. Eastham, MD, chief of the urology service, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. A higher level early in life is a strong signal that you need to be really diligent about checking your PSA.

It has been revealed that “We’ve watched prostate cancer incidence increase—especially metastatic cancer, for over a decade now,” claims Dr. Nyame. “And to know that we have a guideline that is so action-oriented toward reversing that course is really exciting.”.

Marty Munson, right now the health director of Men's Health, has been a health editor at properties including Marie Claire, Prevention, Shape and RealAge. She's also certified as a swim and triathlon coach.

#5362. Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (989 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities.
  • According to recent reports, designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat.
  • “Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang stated in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities. They’ve already experimented with stretching lab-grown human skin over robot faces and with a synthetic hydrogel skin that lets robots really “feel” burns and cuts. Now, a team of engineers at the University of Pennsylvania wants to dig under the skin. In a  study published this week in Advanced Functional Materials, the team describes a highly controllable artificial robot muscle inspired by the small muscles in human eyes and fingers. They put them to the test by having a robot hand strike piano keys at varying intensities and made a set of human eye muscles able to maintain a gaze. It all feels quite uncomfortably adjacent to the 1973 sci-fi film and HBO series Westworld.

According to recent reports, designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat. For starters, most large robots today, especially humanoid ones, rely on bulky, rigid motors and components. That’s fine for more straightforward actions like walking and lifting, but recreating the muscles that move our eyes or fingers requires far more delicate precision. In this case, the engineers needed a material that prioritized flexibility and fine control while staying strong enough to hold up after repeated use. As with many aspects of robotics, tasks that seem quite easy for humans to do are actually often the most difficult tasks for machines. While bipedal robots have been pulling off dance routines and performing acrobatics worth of a Marvel superhero for years, they still fall flat when it comes to something as simple as folding laundry or holding a gaze.

“Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang stated in a statement.

For their muscle fiber, the team settled on liquid crystal elastomers (LCE) combined with graphene and an embedded ultrathin copper coil. The LCE, a rubber-like material, acts as the actual muscle, both contracting and stretching. The graphene serves as a reinforcer, making the material both a bit softer and tougher, so it holds up even when opposing muscles pull in other directions. Together, these two ingredients can produce movement, but on their own they struggle to stay put. When heated, the LCE stretches but then keeps contracting, eventually creeping back toward its original length as it rapidly cools. That’s a problem for subtle movements like holding a gaze or pressing a piano key with light, steady force, where the muscle needs to hold a precise position over a period of time.

It has been revealed that that’s where the coil comes in. The team added the coil inside the fiber to serve as a kind of temperature gauge, and the sensors determine when the muscle is losing heat and contracting. With those readings, the team could then gradually increase temperature to ensure the muscle held its position.

Industry observers note that “We used the resistance of the embedded copper coil as a feedback signal and adjusted the heating power in real time to keep the resistance near a target value,” added study co-author and University of Pennsylvania Ph.D. student Xuelin Wu. “Because the coil served as both a heater and a sensor, we did not need a separate sensor for feedback.”.

Sources indicate that with their artificial muscle designed, it was time to test it in real-world scenarios. First, the team fitted the muscles into a 3D-printed robot hand built to mimic finger movement. They then made the fingers press various piano keys at different levels of force and speed. Sensors placed on the bottom of the keys were able to tell how hard each note was played. The detached hand was no Mozart, but it worked.

Next, they mounted a pair of robotic eyeballs on freely rotating ball joints inside 3D-printed shells. The muscle fibers were attached around the edges of opposing pairs, which were meant to mimic how muscles in the eyes stretch and contract. In testing, the eyes shifted their gaze on demand, with controlled, repeatable movements. The resulting video demonstration is both impressive and unsettling.

According to recent reports, the research joins a growing field of labs and companies racing to build artificial muscle systems. In 2025, Polish startup Clone Robotics took the idea to an extreme with a horrifying video of a faceless, human-sized robot dangling from a ceiling and writhing, its movements supposedly powered by synthetic muscles and a hydraulic system meant to mimic human muscles and blood vessels. They call  their creation the world’s first “musculoskeletal android.” Though it is likely that their video was more a shocking proof-of-concept than an actively working prototype, it nonetheless provides a glimpse into a potentially unsettling future where robots replace mechanical motors and actuators with more human-like muscle fibers.

Protoclone, the world's first bipedal, musculoskeletal android. pic.twitter.com/oIV1yaMSyE.

In a recent development, the University of Pennsylvania researchers say the next step is combining more of these muscles into larger, integrated systems, where dozens of small muscles have to work together to produce more natural expressions. Down the line, they’re interested in potentially using AI computer vision to coordinate those into even more complex systems. Authenticity is the point. The long-term goal, they note, is to create robots that look and feel more and more like the real thing.

“I’m excited about the possibility of using this approach to create robots that move with the same subtlety and expressiveness we see in human faces,” concluded University of Pennsylvania engineer and paper co-author Ziyun Zhang.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we haven’t timed one, but eyeballing it, the Scion Kei-01 should reach its top speed before the 1250-hp Chevy Corvette ZR1X reaches 100 mph. (You’re welcome, Toyota marketing team.) Of course, that’s because America’s newest and cutest truck is limited to just 25 mph, per the feds’ FMVSS No. 500 regulation that allows the Kei-01 to be sold here. Toyota is assembling and selling these rebadged Daihatsu Hijets in the United States starting next year, and we got to take one for a short drive—which will be most drives in a pickup this small—to see whether it lives up to the hype.

First, we had to fight our instinct to get into the driver’s seat from the left side. The Kei-01 is right-hand drive, like the Hijet sold in Japan, because Toyota wanted to bring it to the United States as quickly and inexpensively as possible. Production models will get a different backup camera to meet federal requirements, but beyond that, the U.S. version is largely unchanged from the Daihatsu sold in Japan.

See all results for upcoming 2028 Toyota Scion KEI-01 for sale near 95051.

Sources indicate that every Kei-01 sold here, mainly to fleets, will have an extended cab, which affords extra cargo space for a shotgun or your largest bushel of chewing tobacco. Or both. The fixed steering column doesn’t tilt or telescope, but stovepipe-hat enthusiasts—and it’s been a while since they’ve heard this—have reason to celebrate, as the one thing this truck does big is headroom.

The Kei-01’s “jumbo” cab is why it stands just 2.9 inches lower in height than an F-150, but it’s a lot easier to get into. You barely have to lift a foot to climb in. A portion of the footwell is painted metal, and your feet are ahead of the front wheel wells. The front axle is practically beneath your butt.

In a recent development, unlike the workaday pickups you can rent from Home Depot and Menards, this truck, with its massive screen and power windows, is an ergonomic miracle compared with single-cab full-size rentals. Remember when steering wheels were only responsible for turning left and right and occasionally honking the horn? The Kei-01’s wheel is like that. Except the horn’s high-pitched beep is too humiliating to use in anger.

According to recent reports, your fingertips on the steering wheel are so close to the front of the vehicle that they could almost be the hood ornament. Which is certainly novel and makes it super easy to nose in close to objects. Though the lack of a crumple zone aft of your knuckles is a concern that flashes through your mind.

Sources indicate that around the little dirt loop, the Kei-01 offers a driving feel that’s akin to a riding lawn mower. The steering takes nearly 4.5 turns lock-to-lock, but the Kei-01 is still stupid-easy to maneuver. There’s a rawness about scooting around in it that makes you feel like you’re getting paid hourly. This workhorse may be at a speed disadvantage compared to most of the electric scooters in our Gear Team’s roundup, but try hauling hay with one of those.

See all results for fresh 2028 Toyota Scion KEI-01 for sale near 95051.

Underneath all that adorable sheetmetal is a 660-cc three-cylinder engine that sounds about as smooth as a Honda Grom. It’s paired with a continuously variable automatic transmission. Despite its goofy proportions, the Kei-01 isn’t as front-heavy as it looks. With the engine mounted near the middle of the truck, this little box on wheels feels balanced. It lacks a dedicated transfer case, but its four-wheel-drive system has an electronic lock mode to add a bit more confidence on hill climbs.

In a recent development, the best part might be the roughly five-and-a-half-foot bed. Its low load floor makes for a perfect bench, and all three bedsides fold down. Lower the tailgate, or either side, or all three. It’s brilliantly simple and quick. There’s no tall bedside to reach over, and you don’t have to climb into the bed to reach stuff. The truck can handle 600 pounds of cargo too. Seriously, why can’t full-size pickup beds offer this kind of flexibility?

Recent findings suggest that we spent only a short time driving the little Kei-01, but even limited to 25 mph, it’s still rather compelling. And, unlike the used kei trucks imported from Japan, the Scion has a factory warranty. The big unknown still hanging over this small truck is the price, which Toyota hasn’t unveiled yet. When all you need is a little truck, without most of the drawbacks of a big one, the Kei-01 certainly fits.

Austin Irwin has worked for Car and Driver for over 10 years in various roles. He's steadily worked his way from an entry-level data entry position into driving vehicles for photography and video, and is now reviewing and testing cars. What will he do next? Who knows, but he better be fast.

Driving the Scion Kei Truck: Fun, But Not a Real Solution for Most Americans

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What started as a government-subsidized program to provide cheap, industrious transportation for a Japanese economy that had been ravaged by World War II has become a genuine American fixation.
  • Sources indicate that as with all vehicles not originally built to U.S.
  • Officially known as the Scion by Toyota Kei-01, the rebadged Daihatsu Hijet is powered by a 660-cc three-cylinder gasoline engine making around 53 hp, which is fed through a continuously variable automatic transmission.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What started as a government-subsidized program to provide cheap, industrious transportation for a Japanese economy that had been ravaged by World War II has become a genuine American fixation. In mountainous resort towns in Colorado, Faulkner farmland in the Delta, and Northeast metropolises, the pint-size Kei truck has become a popular target for importers bringing examples from Japan. Now Toyota is set to dump fuel on that fire, as a brand-fresh kei truck from the resurrected Scion brand will be offered in the U.S. market in 2027.

Sources indicate that as with all vehicles not originally built to U.S. standards, federal Department of Transportation rules have limited American kei enthusiasts to importing 25-year-old examples of the miniature trucks. To be frank, most of these tired examples drive as one would expect of a work truck with a quarter century under its belt. Toyota’s incoming example is the exact opposite, as I got the chance to find out during a half-dozen laps of a half-mile cone course at Eagles Canyon Raceway outside Dallas.

Officially known as the Scion by Toyota Kei-01, the rebadged Daihatsu Hijet is powered by a 660-cc three-cylinder gasoline engine making around 53 hp, which is fed through a continuously variable automatic transmission. The Kei-01 is limited to 25 mph, far short of the 70 mph or so a Japanese-market Hijet can accomplish. That threshold was deliberately chosen to comply with federal safety requirements for low-speed vehicles, which mandate that the vehicle go faster than 20 mph but not faster than 25.

Yet that modest limit didn’t mean acceleration was lacking. When I moved the hilariously toylike shifter into drive and matted the gas, the Kei-01 jumped off the line like a puppy smelling sausages, growling and uncoordinated. The lack of gear ratios kept the tiny engine at high rpm, although the missing tach meant I couldn’t verify how fast it was spinning. Regardless, maximum speed was easily reached, according to the speedometer displaying kilometers per hour.

According to recent reports, the ergonomics of a kei truck meant I sat on top of the front wheels and had the Toyota-badged steering wheel tilted into my lap. Also, this being a product designed for the Japanese market, the steering wheel was positioned on the right; Toyota has no aims to reverse the layout for us. With 14-inch wheels and what are barely soccer-ball-diameter tires, the Kei-01 was agile to a fault; I suspect you could pretty much turn it inside a single Costco parking space. Directional changes happened rapidly, although the steering is high geared, and even slow-speed maneuvers elicited a special charm. That remarked, I wouldn’t want to haul it around a tight corner at any rate of speed. And the ride quality could be described generously as rudimentary. I bounced up and down in my adjustable seat over Toyota’s provided gravel course, the interior loudly rattling the whole time. However, as a dedicated work truck, this was hardly disqualifying.

In a recent development, A button in the center console promised locking four-wheel-drive, though I didn’t get to use it. Slowing the Kei-01, with its curb weight of just over 2000 pounds, was as easy as letting off the accelerator. But front disc and rear drum brakes seemed powerful enough. Considering the modest limiter, you could just yank the analog, wire-operated parking brake.

Toyota hasn’t skimped on features. A central touchscreen tucked into the dashboard will supposedly have Apple CarPlay functionality when the Kei-01 arrives in the U.S. next year. Push-button start and slider-style climate controls will also be fitted as standard. For those who have bemoaned the rise of haptic-touch features, the Kei-01 will be the freshest breath of interior design air you’ve had in some time. Icons on the Kei-01’s dashboard even promised ADAS features like lane-departure control and collision warnings. Some of the touch surfaces were hard, and the doors felt featherlight, but who really cares?

Sources indicate that the Kei-01’s payload capacity, scaled to its diminutive dimensions, is just 600 pounds. But the three sides of the load bed can be folded down separately, boosting utility, meaning that trips to Home Depot are more likely to be limited by speed than cargo weight. A storage deck behind the seats is well suited for backpacks and toolboxes, and there are flat storage spaces on the dashboard and built into the roofline.

In a recent development, before you check your credit score, there is a brutal catch to the possibility of buying the Kei-01. Toyota has said it won’t sell the vehicle to individuals initially, with access limited to fleet operators.

In a recent development, the plan is to target luxury resorts, university administrations, and other institutions with the need for such compact utility. This makes sense given both the likely lack of profit in individual trucks and the logic of putting the trucks into the hands of what are likely to be safe, responsible customers with their own private road networks. Toyota hasn’t revealed pricing yet, but the Kei-01 will almost certainly carry a sizable upcharge over the equivalent Hijet, which costs about $9000 in Japan, with U.S. versions being built in Indiana.

It has been revealed that the brutal truth is that a maximum speed of 25 mph means the Scion Kei-01 simply isn’t suited to road use in much of the U.S. Even in the center of cities like New York, where speed limits are largely set at that number, traffic normally flows considerably faster when free to do so. The prospect of trying to drive a Kei-01 on a faster-flowing highway surrounded by inattentive traffic is slightly terrifying. Toyota’s decision to keep the bulk of Kei-01s away from public roads is prudent, if a little disappointing. I’ve never had more fun going 25 mph.

#5357. Psychological Richness: The Third Dimension of a Good Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1190 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Psychological Richness: The Third Dimension of a Good Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Imagine two people sitting at a quiet neighbourhood wine bar on a Tuesday night.
  • It has been revealed that one has spent the last five years carefully pruning their life into a low-friction masterpiece.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Imagine two people sitting at a quiet neighbourhood wine bar on a Tuesday night.

It has been revealed that one has spent the last five years carefully pruning their life into a low-friction masterpiece. A dependable job with Sunday meal prep, and a tight circle of friends with minimal drama.

The other has spent those same five years changing industries, moving apartments twice, taking a solo trip where their luggage got lost in a country whose language they didn't speak, and surviving a breakup that rearranged their entire worldview.

In a recent development, if you asked someone coming from a traditional psychology background who is winning at life, they would likely give you two ways to score it. For over 40 years, researchers have treated a “good life” as a debate between two competing ideals.

On the one side is happiness (i.e., hedonic well-being): a life defined by comfort, stability, positive emotions, and a relative absence of stress. On the other is meaning (i.e., eudaimonic well-being): a life built on purpose, routine, coherence, and contributing to something larger than yourself.

For many, those two ingredients describe a lot. Plenty of people genuinely thrive on straightforward, comfortable lives anchored in meaningful contributions.

Sources indicate that but think about the difference between someone who flourishes in the steady, familiar rhythm of a small town versus someone who only feels fully awake amid the unpredictable friction of a big city. If your primary goal is comfort and coherence, keeping your life simple works.

Alas, that doesn’t describe everyone.

Recent findings suggest that I have spent years trying to figure out why that two-door framework never fully made sense to me. Having things straightforward has never reliably led me to a long-term sense of “good.” Whenever my life becomes too predictable, too frictionless, or too cleanly resolved—when every week looks like a neatly organized calendar block—I don’t feel serene. I feel strangely flat.

It turns out there's a reason that type of restlessness doesn't fit neatly into the classic binary. Psychologist Shigehiro Oishi and colleagues have spent the past several years making the case that we have missed talking about a third dimension of a good life: psychological richness.

In a recent development, oishi defines a psychologically rich life as one filled with diverse, interesting experiences that fundamentally shift one's perspective. Unlike happiness and meaning—which are predicted by personality traits like conscientiousness, agreeableness, and emotional stability, as well as a preference for familiarity and tradition—psychological richness is driven by openness to experience and curiosity. It’s why a bizarre detour on a whim or getting immersed in a dense literary novel can make some people feel deeply alive even if it has zero connection to a five-year initiative.

Sources indicate that in their paper, Oishi and Westgate refer to happiness, meaning, and psychological richness as three “paths” to a good life. Personally, I think calling them paths makes it sound like you have to stand at a fork in the road, pick one direction, and leave the others behind. To me, a more coherent way to understand how these three elements actually work together is through music.

If your life is an album unfolding over time, happiness is harmony. It’s the consonant, pleasant chords that feel warm and uplifting in the moment.

Meaning is the rhythm section. It’s the steady bass line and recurring beat that give pieces structure, direction, and momentum. If you only optimize for harmony and rhythm, you can write clean, catchy pop songs in 4/4 time and play them happily for decades.

Recent findings suggest that but there’s also that third consideration of psychological richness: the structural complexity of the composition. It’s the odd time signature, the unexpected key change, the dissonant bridge that introduces tension and forces you to lean forward because the arrangement refuses to stay predictable.

Once you hear life as an album rather than a linear path, something counterintuitive clicks into place: miserable, frustrating, or unwanted experiences can still make a life deeply worthwhile.

In music, dissonance doesn’t have to be a mistake; it can be what gives a resolution its emotional weight. Research suggests that difficult or disruptive events—heavy workloads, culture shock, failed mountain-climbing attempts, or even recovering from a serious illness—routinely increase psychological richness even while actively tanking day-to-day happiness. When researchers analyzed New York Times obituaries, lives rated high in psychological richness were actually negatively correlated with perceived happiness. You don't have to sit with the ringing of a dissonant chord for it to make the rest of the track unforgettable.

Sources indicate that an appetite for complexity doesn't just leave someone with interesting stories. The research suggests that people leading psychologically rich lives score significantly higher in cognitive complexity, specifically attributional complexity and holistic thinking, even after statistically controlling for baseline openness to experience.

Attributional complexity is the ability to hold multiple, competing explanations in your head at once, to see the invisible situational pressures, systemic context, and messy human contradictions driving someone’s behaviour. Holistic thinking is hearing how the entire arrangement fits together rather than isolating a single note.

It has been revealed that that's why low-complexity thinkers aren't drawn to psychological richness. When someone cuts them off in traffic, or ghosts them after three great dates, or makes a baffling career pivot, a low-complexity thinker reaches for a tidy, single-cause label.

According to recent reports, straightforward lives rarely ask your brain to stretch. When everything resolves cleanly on the downbeat, your brain gets to run on autopilot, relying on familiar scripts and neat categories. You stay comfortable, you stay coherent, but your worldview stops expanding.

Sources indicate that I used to think my dissatisfaction with simple, linear progress meant I was bad at being content—or worse, that I was needlessly complicating a perfectly good groove. Framing it through psychological richness changes how I am able to reckon with these feelings.

In a recent development, some people are built for a clean, consonant melody. There’s real beauty in that. But if you, like me, are wired for cognitive complexity, a life without friction, surprise, and perspective shifts won't feel like peace. It will feel under-composed.

When harmony, rhythm, and complexity all show up in the same piece, it can feel like magic. But if your life feels less like a tidy, predictable tune and more like an intricate arrangement you’re still learning how to play, it doesn’t have to mean you’re failing at living the good life.

It just means that you’re writing a song that is deeply your own.

In a recent development, oishi, S., et al. (2019). The psychologically rich life questionnaire. Journal of Research in Personality, 81, 257–270.

Oishi, S., & Westgate, E. C. (2022). A psychologically rich life: Beyond happiness and meaning. Psychological Review, 129, 790–811.

According to recent reports, oishi, S., et al. (2024). The cognitive complexity of a happy life, a meaningful life, and a psychologically rich life. Journal of Research in Personality, 110, 104475.

#5356. Latest Update: The mysterious golden shipwreck that led to decades of lawsuits

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1126 w)
